Jianliang Qian, Timo Sprekeler, Hung V. Tran, Yifeng Yu J. Qian Department of Mathematics, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI 48824, USA Email address: jqian@msu.edu T. Sprekeler Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore, 10 Lower Kent Ridge Road, Singapore 119076 Email address: timo.sprekeler@nus.edu.sg H. V. Tran Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin Madison, Van Vleck Hall, 480 Lincoln Drive, Madison, Wisconsin 53706, USA Email address: hung@math.wisc.edu Y. Abstract.

We study the optimal rate of convergence in periodic homogenization of the viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation utε+H⁡(xε,D​uε)=ε​Δ​uεu^{\varepsilon}_{t}+H(\frac{x}{\varepsilon},Du^{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon\Delta u^{\varepsilon} in ℝn×(0,∞)\mathbb{R}^{n}\times(0,\infty) subject to a given initial datum. We prove that ‖uε−u‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,T])≤C⁡(1+T)​ε\|u^{\varepsilon}-u\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T])}\leq C(1+T)\sqrt{\varepsilon} for any given T>0T>0, where uu is the viscosity solution of the effective problem. Moreover, we show that the O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) rate is optimal for a natural class of HH and a Lipschitz continuous initial datum, both theoretically and through numerical experiments. It remains an interesting question to investigate whether the convergence rate can be improved when HH is uniformly convex. Finally, we propose a numerical scheme for the approximation of the effective Hamiltonian based on a finite element approximation of approximate corrector problems.

Key words and phrases: 
Periodic homogenization; optimal rate of convergence; second-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations; cell problems; vanishing viscosity process; viscosity solutions
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B10, 35B27, 35B40, 35F21, 49L25

1. Introduction

1.1. Settings

For each ε>0\varepsilon>0, let uε∈C⁡(ℝn×[0,∞))u^{\varepsilon}\in C(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty)) be the viscosity solution to

(1.1) {utε+H⁡(xε,D​uε)=ε​Δ​uεin​ℝn×(0,∞),uε​(x,0)=g⁡(x)on​ℝn.\begin{cases}u_{t}^{\varepsilon}+H\left(\frac{x}{\varepsilon},Du^{\varepsilon}\right)=\varepsilon\Delta u^{\varepsilon}\qquad&\text{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{n}\times(0,\infty),\\ u^{\varepsilon}(x,0)=g(x)\qquad&\text{on}\ \mathbb{R}^{n}.\end{cases}

Here, g∈C0,1​(ℝn)g\in C^{0,1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is a given initial datum and H=H⁡(y,p)∈Liploc​(ℝn×ℝn)H=H(y,p)\in{\rm Lip\,}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}) is a given Hamiltonian that is ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-periodic in its yy-variable and satisfies

(1.2) ess​infy∈ℝn⁡{|H⁡(y,p)|2+(n+1)​Dy​H​(y,p)⋅p}⟶∞as ​|p|→∞.\displaystyle\essinf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left\{|H(y,p)|^{2}+(n+1)D_{y}H(y,p)\cdot p\right\}\longrightarrow\infty\quad\text{as }|p|\rightarrow\infty.

Then, it is known that uεu^{\varepsilon} converges to u∈C⁡(ℝn×[0,∞))u\in C(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty)) locally uniformly on ℝn×[0,∞)\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty) as ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+}, where uu is the viscosity solution to the effective problem

(1.3) {ut+H¯​(D​u)=0in​ℝn×(0,∞),u⁡(x,0)=g⁡(x)on​ℝn;\begin{cases}u_{t}+\overline{H}\left(Du\right)=0\qquad&\text{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{n}\times(0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)=g(x)\qquad&\text{on}\ \mathbb{R}^{n};\end{cases}

see [21, 8]. Here, the effective Hamiltonian H¯∈C⁡(ℝn)\overline{H}\in C(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is determined by HH in a nonlinear way through cell problems. It is worth noting that if H=H⁡(y,p)H=H(y,p) is independent of yy, that is, H⁡(y,p)=F⁡(p)H(y,p)=F(p), then (1.1) becomes the usual vanishing viscosity problem

(1.4) {utε+F⁡(D​uε)=ε​Δ​uεin​ℝn×(0,∞),uε​(x,0)=g⁡(x)on​ℝn,\begin{cases}u_{t}^{\varepsilon}+F\left(Du^{\varepsilon}\right)=\varepsilon\Delta u^{\varepsilon}\qquad&\text{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{n}\times(0,\infty),\\ u^{\varepsilon}(x,0)=g(x)\qquad&\text{on}\ \mathbb{R}^{n},\end{cases}

in which case we have H¯=F\overline{H}=F. Both (1.1) and (1.4) are basic and fundamentally important problems in the theory of viscosity solutions.

Introducing the notation 𝕋n:=ℝn/ℤn\mathbb{T}^{n}:=\mathbb{R}^{n}/\mathbb{Z}^{n}, we now give a precise definition of H¯\overline{H}.

Definition 1 (Effective Hamiltonian).

Assume (A1)–(A2). For each p∈ℝnp\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, there exists a unique constant H¯​(p)∈ℝ\overline{H}(p)\in\mathbb{R} such that the cell (ergodic) problem

(1.5) H⁡(y,p+D​v)=H¯​(p)+Δ​vfor​y∈𝕋n\qquad H(y,p+Dv)=\overline{H}(p)+\Delta v\qquad\text{for}\ y\in\mathbb{T}^{n}

has a continuous viscosity solution vv. If needed, we write v=v⁡(y,p)v=v(y,p) or v=vp​(y)v=v_{p}(y) to clearly demonstrate the nonlinear dependence of vv on pp. In the literature, v⁡(⋅,p)v(\cdot,p) is often called a corrector. It is worth mentioning that v⁡(⋅,p)v(\cdot,p) is unique up to additive constants.

From now on, we normalize the corrector vv so that v⁡(0,p)=0v(0,p)=0 for all p∈ℝnp\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. In fact, v⁡(⋅,p)∈C2​(𝕋n)v(\cdot,p)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{n}) and p↦v⁡(⋅,p)p\mapsto v(\cdot,p) is locally Lipschitz. Further, the effective Hamiltonian H¯\overline{H} is locally Lipschitz.

Our main goal in this paper is to obtain the optimal rate for the convergence of uεu^{\varepsilon} to uu, that is, an optimal bound for ‖uε−u‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,T])\|u^{\varepsilon}-u\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T])} for any given T>0T>0 as ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+}. Heuristically, thanks to the two-scale asymptotic expansion,

(1.6) uε​(x,t)≈u⁡(x,t)+ε​v​(xε,D​u​(x,t))+O⁡(ε2).u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)\approx u(x,t)+\varepsilon v\left(\frac{x}{\varepsilon},Du(x,t)\right)+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

However, this is just a formal local expansion, and it is not clear at all how to obtain the optimal global bound in the L∞L^{\infty}-norm from this.

1.2. Main results

We now describe our main results. Let us introduce the set of assumptions (A1)–(A3) given by

  • (A1)

    H∈Liploc​(ℝn×ℝn)H\in{\rm Lip\,}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}), and H⁡(⋅,p)H(\cdot,p) is ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-periodic for each p∈ℝnp\in\mathbb{R}^{n};

  • (A2)

    HH satisfies (1.2);

  • (A3)

    g∈Lip⁡(ℝn)g\in{\rm Lip\,}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with ‖g‖C0,1​(ℝn)<∞\|g\|_{C^{0,1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}<\infty.

Theorem 1.1.

Assume (A1)–(A3) and fix T>0T>0. Then, there exists a constant C>0C>0 depending only on HH, nn, and ‖g‖C0,1​(ℝn)\|g\|_{C^{0,1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})} such that for ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) there holds

‖uε−u‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,T])≤C⁡(1+T)​ε,\|u^{\varepsilon}-u\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T])}\leq C(1+T)\sqrt{\varepsilon},

where uεu^{\varepsilon} and uu denote the viscosity solutions to (1.1) and (1.3), respectively.

The above rate O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) turns out to be optimal in the sense that there exist particular choices of HH and gg satisfying (A1)–(A3) such that the convergence rate is exactly O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}). Quantitative homogenization for Hamilton-Jacobi equations in the periodic setting has received quite a lot of attention in the past twenty years. The convergence rate O⁡(ε1/3)O(\varepsilon^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}}) was obtained for first-order equations first in [5]. In [3], the authors generalized the method in [5] to get the same convergence rate O⁡(ε1/3)O(\varepsilon^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}}) for the viscous case considered in this paper. For weakly coupled systems of first-order equations, see [24]. For other related works, see the references in [5, 3, 24]. Of course, the rate O⁡(ε1/3)O(\varepsilon^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}}) is not known to be optimal in general.

The optimal rate of convergence O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) for convex first-order equations was recently obtained in [34]. Moreover, we expect that for any given uniformly convex HH, the convergence rate is O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) for (1.1) for generic initial data, which is stronger than the notion of optimality in this paper. We refer to [16] for the multi-scale setting. For earlier progress in this direction with nearly optimal rates of convergence, we refer the reader to [25, 35, 23, 6] and the references therein. To date, optimal rates of convergence for general nonconvex first-order cases have not been established.

To the best of our knowledge, the optimal rate of convergence for periodic homogenization of viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations has not been obtained in the current literature. The rate O⁡(ε1/3)O(\varepsilon^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}}) was obtained in [5, 3] by using the doubling variable technique, the perturbed test function method [8], and the approximate cell problems. The usage of the approximate cell problems introduces another parameter in the analysis, and as a result, the rate O⁡(ε1/3)O(\varepsilon^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}}) was the best one can obtain through this route by optimizing over all parameters.

In this paper, we are able to obtain the O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) convergence rate by dealing directly with the correctors. A key point is that after normalizing v⁡(0,p)=0v(0,p)=0, we have that v⁡(⋅,p)v(\cdot,p) is unique, and p↦v⁡(⋅,p)p\mapsto v(\cdot,p) is locally Lipschitz. It is worth noting that we do not require convexity of the Hamiltonian in Theorem 1.1.

Here, we will use H⁡(y,p)=F⁡(p)H(y,p)=F(p) for some choices of nonlinear FF to construct computable sharp examples. Similar results were known for linear FF in the context of conservation laws [30]. The connection between scalar conservation laws and Hamilton-Jacobi equations is well known to experts. Precisely speaking, in one dimension, if u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) is a viscosity solution to ut+F⁡(ux)=0u_{t}+F(u_{x})=0, then v=uxv=u_{x} is an entropy solution to vt+(F⁡(v))x=0v_{t}+(F(v))_{x}=0. The convergence rate of vanishing viscosity in scalar conservation laws has been well studied and the convergence rate of O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) was known under suitable assumptions [18].

Theorem 1.2.

Let n=1n=1. Let F∈Liploc​(ℝ)F\in{\rm Lip\,}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}) be such that

{F⁡(p)=p for p∈[0,1],F⁡(p)≤p for p∈[−1,0],\begin{cases}F(p)=p\qquad&\text{ for $p\in[0,1]$},\\ F(p)\leq p\qquad&\text{ for $p\in[-1,0]$},\end{cases}

and suppose that g⁡(x)=max⁡{1−|x|,0}g(x)=\max\{1-|x|,0\} for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Then, for any ε∈(0,14)\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{4}) there holds

|uε​(0,1)−u⁡(0,1)|≥e−1π​e​ε,|u^{\varepsilon}(0,1)-u(0,1)|\geq\frac{\mathrm{e}-1}{\sqrt{\pi}\mathrm{e}}\sqrt{\varepsilon},

where uεu^{\varepsilon} denotes the viscosity solution to (1.4) and uu denotes the viscosity solution to (1.3) with H¯=F\overline{H}=F.

We would like to point out that the above gg can be replaced by a smooth function (Remark 1). Also, the proof of Theorem 1.2 leads to the following corollary.

Corollary 1.3.

Let n=1n=1. Assume that F∈Liploc​(ℝ)F\in{\rm Lip\,}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}) and that FF is linear in (a,b)⊂ℝ(a,b)\subset\mathbb{R} for some given a<ba<b. Then, there exists an initial datum g∈Lip⁡(ℝ)g\in{\rm Lip\,}(\mathbb{R}) such that for any ε∈(0,14)\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{4}) we have that

|uε​(0,1)−u⁡(0,1)|≥c0​ε|u^{\varepsilon}(0,1)-u(0,1)|\geq c_{0}\sqrt{\varepsilon}

for some constant c0>0c_{0}>0 depending only on FF and gg, where uεu^{\varepsilon} denotes the viscosity solution to (1.4) and uu denotes the viscosity solution to (1.3) with H¯=F\overline{H}=F.

It is also straightforward to generalize Theorem 1.2 to any dimension in the corollary below, whose proof is essentially the same as that of Theorem 1.2.

Corollary 1.4.

Let F∈Liploc​(ℝn)F\in{\rm Lip\,}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) be such that

{F⁡(s​e1)=s for s∈[0,1],F⁡(s​e1)≤s for s∈[−1,0],\begin{cases}F(se_{1})=s\qquad&\text{ for $s\in[0,1]$},\\ F(se_{1})\leq s\qquad&\text{ for $s\in[-1,0]$},\end{cases}

and suppose that g⁡(x)=max⁡{1−|x1|,0}g(x)=\max\{1-|x_{1}|,0\} for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then, for any ε∈(0,14)\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{4}) there holds

|uε​(0,1)−u⁡(0,1)|≥e−1π​e​ε,|u^{\varepsilon}(0,1)-u(0,1)|\geq\frac{\mathrm{e}-1}{\sqrt{\pi}\mathrm{e}}\sqrt{\varepsilon},

where uεu^{\varepsilon} denotes the viscosity solution to (1.4) and uu denotes the viscosity solution to (1.3) with H¯=F\overline{H}=F.

The bound O⁡(T​ε)O(\sqrt{T\varepsilon}) for ‖uε−u‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,T])\|u^{\varepsilon}-u\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T])} for the vanishing viscosity process of (1.4) was obtained in [11, 7, 9]. In this situation, we only need to assume that FF is locally Lipschitz on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and gg is bounded and Lipschitz on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} (see e.g., [7, Theorem 5.1]). For the static cases, see [32, 33].

Thus, the results of Theorem 1.2 and Corollaries 1.3–1.4 confirm both the optimality of the convergence rate of the vanishing viscosity process of (1.4) with optimal conditions, and the optimality of the O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) bound in Theorem 1.1. See Remark 1 for Theorem 1.2 with a C2C^{2} initial condition for each ε>0\varepsilon>0. Besides, we provide a generalization of Theorem 1.2 in Proposition 4.2 in which for each fixed ε∈(0,14)\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{4}), the Hamiltonian FF needs not to be linear in any interval in one dimension at the price of nonconvexity. Note also that in Corollary 1.4, FF does not need to be linear in any open set in multiple dimensions.

Note that all the Hamiltonians in Theorem 1.2 and Corollaries 1.3–1.4 are not strictly convex and do not have yy-dependence (i.e., no homogenization effect is involved). Hence, it is natural to ask (I) whether the convergence rate can be improved for strictly/uniformly convex HH and (II) how the yy-dependence impacts the convergence rate.

(I) has been investigated in the context of one dimensional conservation laws for the vanishing viscosity process of (1.4). It was proved that the convergence rate can be improved to O⁡(ε​|log⁡ε|)O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|) for uniformly convex FF under some technical assumptions [31]. In Section 4.3, we demonstrate this fact for the quadratic Hamiltonian F⁡(p)=12​|p|2F(p)=\frac{1}{2}|p|^{2} in any dimension for general Lipschitz continuous initial data. More interestingly, we showed that for any C2C^{2} initial datum gg, the convergence rate is O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) for a.e. (x,t)∈ℝn×(0,∞)(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times(0,\infty). For strictly but not uniformly convex FF, numerical computation shows that the convergence rate could be various fractions. For instance, for F⁡(p)=14​|p|4F(p)=\frac{1}{4}|p|^{4} in Example 5, the rate of convergence for the vanishing viscosity process of (1.4) seems to be O⁡(ε2/3)O(\varepsilon^{2/3}). This suggests that there might be a variety of rates O⁡(εs)O(\varepsilon^{s}) for 12≤s≤1\frac{1}{2}\leq s\leq 1 for (1.4), which is a new phenomenon. It will be an interesting project to find an example where a convergence rate α∈(12,1)\alpha\in(\frac{1}{2},1) can be established rigorously.

As for (II), it is quite challenging to conduct a theoretical analysis beyond Theorem 1.1 when yy is present. In this paper, we will focus on numerical computations to get some rough ideas and inspire interested readers to work on this subject. Our numerical Examples 10 and 11 show that when H=H⁡(y,p)H=H(y,p) is strictly convex in pp and smooth in yy, the convergence rate is similar to O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) or O⁡(ε​|log⁡ε|)O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|). Meanwhile, when the regularity in yy is merely Lipschitz continuity, the convergence rate seems to be reduced; see Examples 6 -9.

Finally, we discuss the construction of numerical methods for the approximation of the effective Hamiltonian H¯\overline{H}. In particular, we provide a simple scheme to approximate H¯\overline{H} at a fixed point based on a finite element approximation of approximate corrector problems. For related work on the numerical approximation of effective Hamiltonians we refer to [1, 12, 14, 15, 20, 26] for first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations without viscosity term, and to [13, 17] for second-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman and Isaacs equations.

Organization of the paper

In Section 2, we use a priori estimates to simplify the settings of the problems. The proof of the bound in Theorem 1.1 is given in Section 3. In Section 4, we consider (1.4) with various choices of FF and gg, and obtain the optimality of the bound in Theorem 1.1. In particular, this section includes a proof of Theorem 1.2. Numerical results for both (1.1) and (1.4) are studied in Section 5. The approximation of the effective Hamiltonian is studied in Section 6.

2. Settings and simplifications

Assume (A1)–(A3). For ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), let uεu^{\varepsilon} denote the viscosity solution to (1.1). Let uu denote the viscosity solution to (1.3). By the comparison principle, we have that

(2.1) ‖ut‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,∞))+‖D​u‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,∞))≤M\|u_{t}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty))}+\|Du\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty))}\leq M

for M:=R0+max{|p|≤R0}|H¯(p)|M:=R_{0}+\max_{\{|p|\leq R_{0}\}}|\overline{H}(p)|, where R0:=‖D​g‖L∞​(ℝn)R_{0}:=\|Dg\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}.

Let us further assume that

(2.2) ‖utε‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,∞))+‖D​uε‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,∞))≤C0\|u^{\varepsilon}_{t}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty))}+\|Du^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty))}\leq C_{0}

for a constant C0≥MC_{0}\geq M that is independent of ε\varepsilon. Note that (2.2) is satisfied if g∈C2​(ℝn)g\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with ‖g‖C2​(ℝn)<∞\|g\|_{C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}<\infty, using the classical Bernstein method based on (A1)–(A2). Since gg is merely assumed to be in C0,1​(ℝn)C^{0,1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) in Theorem 1.1, we will employ a suitable mollification of gg in Section 3.2 to remove the assumption (2.2).

Accordingly, values of H⁡(y,p)H(y,p) for |p|>C0|p|>C_{0} are irrelevant. Indeed, letting ξ∈C∞​(ℝn,[0,1])\xi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},[0,1]) be a cut-off function satisfying

ξ⁡(p)=1​ if ​|p|≤C0+1,ξ⁡(p)=0​ if ​|p|≥2​(C0+1),\xi(p)=1\text{ if }|p|\leq C_{0}+1,\qquad\xi(p)=0\text{ if }|p|\geq 2(C_{0}+1),

and introducing

H~​(y,p):=ξ⁡(p)​H​(y,p)+(1−ξ⁡(p))​|p|2 for ​(y,p)∈𝕋n×ℝn,\widetilde{H}(y,p):=\xi(p)H(y,p)+(1-\xi(p))|p|^{2}\quad\text{ for }(y,p)\in\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n},

we have that H~\widetilde{H} satisfies (A1)–(A2) and uεu^{\varepsilon} solves (1.1) with H~\widetilde{H} in place of HH. Therefore, from now on, we can assume that HH takes the form of H~\widetilde{H}, that is, HH satisfies

  • (A4)

    H⁡(y,p)=|p|2H(y,p)=|p|^{2} for y∈𝕋ny\in\mathbb{T}^{n} and |p|≥2​(C0+1)|p|\geq 2(C_{0}+1).

Assumption (A4) helps us simplify the situation quite a bit as follows. For |p|≥2​(C0+1)|p|\geq 2(C_{0}+1), it is clear that v⁡(⋅,p)≡0v(\cdot,p)\equiv 0 and H¯​(p)=|p|2\overline{H}(p)=|p|^{2}. Hence, we obtain that p↦v⁡(⋅,p)p\mapsto v(\cdot,p) is bounded and globally Lipschitz, that is, there exists C>0C>0 such that

(2.3) ∥v(⋅,p)∥L∞​(𝕋n)≤C,∥v(⋅,p)−v(⋅,p~)∥L∞​(𝕋n)≤C|p−p~|∀p,p~∈ℝn.\|v(\cdot,p)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}\leq C,\quad\|v(\cdot,p)-v(\cdot,\tilde{p})\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}\leq C|p-\tilde{p}|\qquad\forall p,\tilde{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

If a function h:ℝn→ℝh:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-periodic, we can think of hh as a function from 𝕋n\mathbb{T}^{n} to ℝ\mathbb{R} as well, and vise versa. In this paper, we switch freely between the two interpretations.

3. Proof of Theorem 1.1

3.1. Part 1: Proof based on (2.2)

Assumptions (A1)–(A4) are always in force in this section. Let T>0T>0 be fixed. Our goal is to show that there exists a constant C>0C>0 depending only on ‖H‖C0,1​(𝕋n×B​(0,2​(C0+1))¯)\|H\|_{C^{0,1}\left(\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\overline{B(0,2(C_{0}+1))}\right)}, nn, and C0C_{0} from (2.2) such that for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) there holds

(3.1) ‖uε−u‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,T])≤C⁡(1+T)​ε.\|u^{\varepsilon}-u\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T])}\leq C(1+T)\sqrt{\varepsilon}.

The approach here is inspired by that in [33, Theorem 4.40]. We first show that

(3.2) uε​(x,t)−u⁡(x,t)≤C⁡(1+T)​ε∀(x,t)∈ℝn×[0,T].\displaystyle u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)-u(x,t)\leq C(1+T)\sqrt{\varepsilon}\qquad\forall(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T].
Proof of (3.2).

We divide the proof into several steps.

Step 0: We write 𝒜:=ℝn×ℝn×ℝn×[0,∞)×[0,∞)\mathcal{A}:=\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty). For K>0K>0 to be chosen and γ∈(0,12)\gamma\in(0,\frac{1}{2}), we introduce the auxiliary function Φ1:𝒜→ℝ\Phi_{1}:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} given by

4. Optimality of the bound in Theorem 1.1

In this section, we consider the vanishing viscosity problem (1.4) with particular choices of FF and gg. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, let uεu^{\varepsilon} denote the viscosity solution to (1.4), and let uu denote the viscosity solution to (1.3) with H¯=F\overline{H}=F. If F∈Liploc​(ℝn)F\in{\rm Lip\,}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and g∈Lip⁡(ℝn)g\in{\rm Lip\,}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), then ‖D​uε‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,∞))≤‖D​g‖L∞​(ℝn)\|Du^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\infty))}\leq\|Dg\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}. Besides, it was obtained in [11, 7, 9] that

(4.1) ‖uε−u‖L∞​(ℝn×[0,T])≤C​T​ε,\|u^{\varepsilon}-u\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T])}\leq C\sqrt{T\varepsilon},

Below, we study both Cauchy problems and Dirichlet problems.

4.1. A linear Cauchy problem

We first consider the case that FF is linear in one dimension.

Proposition 4.1.

=14​π​ε​∫−∞∞e−y24​ε​g~​(y−1)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{y^{2}}{4\varepsilon}}\tilde{g}(y-1)\,\mathrm{d}y

4.3.1. Improvement of convergence rates.

It was shown in [31] that if the Hamiltonian FF is uniformly convex, i.e., F′′≥αF^{\prime\prime}\geq\alpha on ℝ\mathbb{R} for some constant α>0\alpha>0, then the convergence rate of the vanishing viscosity limit can be improved to O⁡(ε​|log⁡ε|)O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|) when the initial datum satisfies certain technical assumptions. Below we show that for F⁡(p)=12​|p|2F(p)=\frac{1}{2}|p|^{2}, the rate is almost everywhere O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) when the initial datum is C2C^{2}, although O⁡(ε​|log⁡ε|)O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|) could happen at some points. For F⁡(p)=12​|p|2F(p)=\frac{1}{2}|p|^{2}, we have by the Hopf-Lax formula (see e.g., [10, 33]) that

u⁡(x,t)=infy∈ℝ{g⁡(y)+t​L​(x−yt)},whereL⁡(v):=supp∈ℝ{p​v−F⁡(p)}=12​|v|2.\displaystyle u(x,t)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{g(y)+t\,L\left(\frac{x-y}{t}\right)\right\},\quad\text{where}\quad L(v):=\sup_{p\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{pv-F(p)\right\}=\frac{1}{2}|v|^{2}.

In particular, for any (x,t)∈ℝ×(0,∞)(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times(0,\infty) there holds

It is not clear to us whether Proposition 4.4 holds for other uniformly convex FF. For strictly but not uniformly convex FF (e.g., F⁡(p)=14​|p|4F(p)=\frac{1}{4}|p|^{4}), the convergence rate for the vanishing viscosity process might be O⁡(εα)O(\varepsilon^{\alpha}) for some exponent α∈(12,1)\alpha\in(\frac{1}{2},1); see the numerical Example 5. A natural question is whether we will see a similar convergence rate when the homogenization process is involved for the quadratic case as numerical Example 10 suggests. Let us briefly demonstrate the technical difficulty in extending the proof of Proposition 4.4 to the homogenization problem. Consider H⁡(y,p)=12​|p|2+V⁡(y)H(y,p)=\frac{1}{2}|p|^{2}+V(y) for a smooth ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-periodic potential function VV. Then, by the Hopf-Cole transformation, we have that

uε​(x,t)=−2​ε​log⁡[h⁡(xε,tε)],u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)=-2\varepsilon\log\left[h\left(\frac{x}{\varepsilon},\frac{t}{\varepsilon}\right)\right],

where h=h⁡(x,t)h=h(x,t) is the solution to the problem

{ht−Δ​h+12​V​h=0in​ℝn×(0,∞),h⁡(x,0)=e−g⁡(ε​x)2​εon​ℝn.\begin{cases}h_{t}-\Delta h+\frac{1}{2}Vh=0\qquad&\text{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{n}\times(0,\infty),\\ h(x,0)=\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{g(\varepsilon x)}{2\varepsilon}}\qquad&\text{on}\ \mathbb{R}^{n}.\end{cases}

Therefore, we have that

uε​(x,t)=−2​ε​log⁡[∫ℝnK⁡(xε,yε,tε)​e−g⁡(y)2​ε​𝑑y],u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)=-2\varepsilon\log\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}K\left(\frac{x}{\varepsilon},\frac{y}{\varepsilon},\frac{t}{\varepsilon}\right)\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{g(y)}{2\varepsilon}}\,\mathrm{d}y\right],

where K=K⁡(x,y,t)K=K(x,y,t) denotes the fundamental solution corresponding to the operator ∂t−Δ+12V\partial_{t}-\Delta+\frac{1}{2}V. Obtaining the convergence rate requires a sharp estimate of the homogenization of KK, which is a highly nontrivial subject. Let us further point out that the convergence rate might also depend on the regularity of VV as the numerical Example 6 suggests.

4.4. A Dirichlet problem

We are again in one dimension. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, we consider the Dirichlet problem

(4.15) {2​(uε)3=ε​(uε)′′ in ​(0,∞),uε​(0)=1.\begin{cases}2(u^{\varepsilon})^{3}=\varepsilon(u^{\varepsilon})^{\prime\prime}\quad\text{ in }(0,\infty),\\ u^{\varepsilon}(0)=1.\end{cases}

It is quickly seen that the solution is given by

uε​(x)=εx+ε for ​x≥0.u^{\varepsilon}(x)=\frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{x+\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\quad\text{ for }x\geq 0.

In particular, we have uε→u≡0u^{\varepsilon}\to u\equiv 0 locally uniformly in (0,∞)(0,\infty). Of course, there is a boundary layer of size O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) at x=0x=0, but let us ignore this boundary layer in our discussion here. We observe that for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) there holds

|uε​(1)−u⁡(1)|=ε1+ε≥12​ε.|u^{\varepsilon}(1)-u(1)|=\frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{1+\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\varepsilon}.

Thus, once again, we see that the O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) rate occurs naturally here. We record this in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.5.

For ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), let uεu^{\varepsilon} denote the solution to (4.15). Then, uε→u≡0u^{\varepsilon}\to u\equiv 0 locally uniformly in (0,∞)(0,\infty), and there holds

|uε​(x)−u⁡(x)|=εx+ε≥12​x​ε∀x≥1.|u^{\varepsilon}(x)-u(x)|=\frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{x+\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\geq\frac{1}{2x}\sqrt{\varepsilon}\qquad\forall x\geq 1.

In particular, for any d>1d>1, the optimal rate for the convergence of uεu^{\varepsilon} to uu in the L∞​((,,,))L^{\infty}((1,d))-norm is O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}).

Since the exact solution to the homogenized problem (1.3) is unknown, we compute ‖uε​(⋅,T)−uε/2​(⋅,T)‖L∞​(Ω)\|u^{\varepsilon}(\cdot,T)-u^{\nicefrac{{\varepsilon}}{{2}}}(\cdot,T)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} for some chosen T>0T>0 and computational domain Ω\Omega.

Example 6.

Assume H⁡(y,p)=12​|p|2+mink∈ℤ⁡|y−k|H(y,p)=\frac{1}{2}|p|^{2}+\min_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}|y-k| for y,p∈ℝy,p\in\mathbb{R}. Numerical results are shown in Figure 5.2 (A). The order of convergence seems to be in [12,23][\frac{1}{2},\frac{2}{3}].

Assume H⁡(y,p)=14​|p|4+mink∈ℤ⁡|y−k|2H(y,p)=\frac{1}{4}|p|^{4}+\min_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}|y-k|^{2} for y,p∈ℝy,p\in\mathbb{R}. Numerical results are shown in Figure 5.2 (D). We observe the same as for Example 7.

Assume H⁡(y,p)=12​|p|2+sin⁡(y)H(y,p)=\frac{1}{2}|p|^{2}+\sin(y) for y,p∈ℝy,p\in\mathbb{R}. Numerical results are shown in Figure 5.2 (E), and the order of convergence seems to be close to 11.

6. Numerical approximation of effective Hamiltonians

In this section, we would like to gain a better understanding of the effective Hamiltonian H¯\overline{H}. Let us recall that for p∈ℝnp\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the value H¯​(p)∈ℝ\overline{H}(p)\in\mathbb{R} is the unique constant for which there exists a viscosity solution v⁡(⋅,p)∈C⁡(𝕋n)v(\cdot,p)\in C(\mathbb{T}^{n}) to

H⁡(y,p+D​v)=H¯​(p)+Δ​vfor​y∈𝕋n.\qquad H(y,p+Dv)=\overline{H}(p)+\Delta v\qquad\text{for}\ y\in\mathbb{T}^{n}.

6.1. Framework

Let us focus on a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman nonlinearity

(6.1) H:𝕋n×ℝn→ℝ,H(y,p):=supα∈Λ{−b(y,α)⋅p−f(y,α)},\displaystyle H:\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\qquad H(y,p):=\sup_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\left\{-b(y,\alpha)\cdot p-f(y,\alpha)\right\},

where Λ\Lambda is a compact metric space, b∈C⁡(𝕋n×Λ,ℝn)b\in C(\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\Lambda;\mathbb{R}^{n}), f∈C⁡(𝕋n×Λ)f\in C(\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\Lambda), and we assume that b=b⁡(y,α)b=b(y,\alpha), f=f⁡(y,α)f=f(y,\alpha) are Lipschitz continuous in yy, uniformly in α\alpha. In this setting, H∈Lip⁡(𝕋n×ℝn)H\in{\rm Lip\,}(\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}) and H=H⁡(y,p)H=H(y,p) is convex in pp. See [22] and the references therein for the homogenization of viscous G-equations.

6.2. Approximation of the effective Hamiltonian

Let p∈ℝnp\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be fixed. Our goal is to approximate the value H¯​(p)\overline{H}(p), and we begin by introducing approximate correctors.

6.2.1. Approximate correctors

For σ>0\sigma>0, introducing the approximate corrector vσ∈C⁡(𝕋n)v^{\sigma}\in C(\mathbb{T}^{n}) to be the unique viscosity solution to the problem

(6.2) σ​vσ+H⁡(y,p+D​vσ)=Δ​vσfor​y∈𝕋n,\displaystyle\sigma v^{\sigma}+H(y,p+Dv^{\sigma})=\Delta v^{\sigma}\qquad\text{for}\ y\in\mathbb{T}^{n},

it is known that {−σ​vσ}σ>0\{-\sigma v^{\sigma}\}_{\sigma>0} converges uniformly to the constant H¯​(p)\overline{H}(p) as σ→0+\sigma\rightarrow 0^{+}; see [19, Chapter 4].

Lemma 6.1.

For σ>0\sigma>0, let vσv^{\sigma} denote the unique viscosity solution to (6.2). Then, vσ∈C2,γ​(𝕋n)v^{\sigma}\in C^{2,\gamma}(\mathbb{T}^{n}) for any γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Moreover, for any σ>0\sigma>0 there holds

‖σ​vσ+H¯​(p)‖L∞​(𝕋n)≤C​σ,\|\sigma v^{\sigma}+\overline{H}(p)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}\leq C\sigma,

where C>0C>0 is a constant independent of σ\sigma.

Proof.

As H∈Lip⁡(𝕋n×ℝn)H\in{\rm Lip\,}(\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}), we have that vσ∈W2,p​(𝕋n)v^{\sigma}\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb{T}^{n}) for any p>1p>1; see [2]. Hence, D​vσ∈C0,γ​(𝕋n)Dv^{\sigma}\in C^{0,\gamma}(\mathbb{T}^{n}) for any γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), and hence, H⁡(⋅,D​vσ​(⋅))∈C0,γ​(𝕋n)H(\cdot,Dv^{\sigma}(\cdot))\in C^{0,\gamma}(\mathbb{T}^{n}). By the standard Schauder estimates, we obtain that vσ∈C2,γ​(𝕋n)v^{\sigma}\in C^{2,\gamma}(\mathbb{T}^{n}).

Let v=v⁡(⋅,p)∈C⁡(𝕋n)v=v(\cdot,p)\in C(\mathbb{T}^{n}) be a solution to the cell problem (1.5). Then, the function v−‖v‖L∞​(𝕋n)−H¯​(p)σv-\|v\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}-\frac{\overline{H}(p)}{\sigma} is a subsolution to (6.2) and the function v+‖v‖L∞​(𝕋n)−H¯​(p)σv+\|v\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}-\frac{\overline{H}(p)}{\sigma} is a supersolution to (6.2). By the comparison principle, we have that

v−‖v‖L∞​(𝕋n)−H¯​(p)σ≤vσ≤v+‖v‖L∞​(𝕋n)−H¯​(p)σin ​𝕋n,v-\|v\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}-\frac{\overline{H}(p)}{\sigma}\leq v^{\sigma}\leq v+\|v\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}-\frac{\overline{H}(p)}{\sigma}\quad\text{in }\mathbb{T}^{n},

and hence,

‖σ​vσ+H¯​(p)‖L∞​(𝕋n)≤2​‖v‖L∞​(𝕋n)​σ,\|\sigma v^{\sigma}+\overline{H}(p)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}\leq 2\|v\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{n})}\sigma,

which completes the proof. ∎

Therefore, a natural idea is to obtain a numerical approximation of H¯​(p)\overline{H}(p) based on the fact that

H¯​(p)=limσ→0+∫Y(−σ​vσ),\displaystyle\overline{H}(p)=\lim_{\sigma\rightarrow 0^{+}}\int_{Y}(-\sigma v^{\sigma}),

where Y:=(0,1)nY:=(0,1)^{n}, in combination with a numerical approximation vhσv^{\sigma}_{h} of vσv^{\sigma} with ‖vσ−vhσ‖L1​(Y)→0\|v^{\sigma}-v^{\sigma}_{h}\|_{L^{1}(Y)}\rightarrow 0 as h→0h\rightarrow 0 for σ\sigma fixed. Let us briefly address a possible numerical approximation for ‖b‖∞\|b\|_{\infty} small. To ensure strong monotonicity of the finite element schemes proposed below, we assume that

(6.3) σ>‖b‖∞24,\displaystyle\sigma>\frac{\|b\|_{\infty}^{2}}{4},

requiring a minimum discount to be imposed for the numerical scheme. Here, we follow the idea of the small-δ\delta method (see, e.g., [26]) in combination with a finite element approximation of (6.2). We note that the effective Hamiltonian can also be approximated by the large-T method; see [26, 27] and the references therein. Since the large-T method and the small-δ\delta method (see, e.g., [26]) are mathematically equivalent, we just use the small-δ\delta method to illustrate the new formulation for convenience.

6.2.2. Hper1​(Y)H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y)-conforming finite element approximation of (6.2)

We have that vσv^{\sigma} is the unique element in Hper1​(Y)H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y) such that

a⁡(vσ,φ)=0∀φ∈Hper1​(Y),\displaystyle a(v^{\sigma},\varphi)=0\qquad\forall\varphi\in H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y),

where a:Hper1​(Y)×Hper1​(Y)→ℝa:H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y)\times H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is given by

a(w,φ):=(Dw,Dφ)L2​(Y)+(supα∈Λ{−b(⋅,α)⋅Dw−g(⋅,α)},φ)L2​(Y)+σ(w,φ)L2​(Y)\displaystyle a(w,\varphi):=(Dw,D\varphi)_{L^{2}(Y)}+(\sup_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\left\{-b(\cdot,\alpha)\cdot Dw-g(\cdot,\alpha)\right\},\varphi)_{L^{2}(Y)}+\sigma(w,\varphi)_{L^{2}(Y)}

with g⁡(⋅,α):=b⁡(⋅,α)⋅p+f⁡(⋅,α)g(\cdot,\alpha):=b(\cdot,\alpha)\cdot p+f(\cdot,\alpha). Indeed, assuming (6.3), a:Hper1​(Y)×Hper1​(Y)→ℝa:H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y)\times H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is strongly monotone since for any u1,u2∈Hper1​(Y)u_{1},u_{2}\in H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y) and s∈(‖b‖∞24​σ,1)s\in(\frac{\|b\|_{\infty}^{2}}{4\sigma},1), writing δu:=u1−u2\delta_{u}:=u_{1}-u_{2},

a⁡(u1,δu)−a⁡(u2,δu)\displaystyle a(u_{1},\delta_{u})-a(u_{2},\delta_{u}) ≥‖D​δu‖L2​(Y)2+σ​‖δu‖L2​(Y)2−(supα∈Λ|b⁡(⋅,α)⋅D​δu|,|δu|)L2​(Y)\displaystyle\geq\|D\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}+\sigma\|\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}-(\sup_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\ \lvert b(\cdot,\alpha)\cdot D\delta_{u}\rvert,\lvert\delta_{u}\rvert)_{L^{2}(Y)}
≥(1−s)​‖D​δu‖L2​(Y)2+(σ−14​s​‖b‖∞2)​‖δu‖L2​(Y)2\displaystyle\geq(1-s)\|D\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}+\left(\sigma-\frac{1}{4s}\|b\|_{\infty}^{2}\right)\|\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}
≥Cm​‖δu‖H1​(Y)2.\displaystyle\geq C_{m}\|\delta_{u}\|_{H^{1}(Y)}^{2}.

It is also quickly checked that we have the Lipschitz property

|a⁡(u1,φ)−a⁡(u2,φ)|≤Cl​‖u1−u2‖H1​(Y)​‖φ‖H1​(Y)∀u1,u2,φ∈Hper1​(Y).\displaystyle\lvert a(u_{1},\varphi)-a(u_{2},\varphi)\rvert\leq C_{l}\|u_{1}-u_{2}\|_{H^{1}(Y)}\|\varphi\|_{H^{1}(Y)}\qquad\forall u_{1},u_{2},\varphi\in H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y).

Let Vh⊂Hper1​(Y)V_{h}\subset H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y) be a closed linear subspace of Hper1​(Y)H^{1}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y). By the Browder-Minty theorem and standard conforming Galerkin arguments, there exists a unique vhσ∈Vhv^{\sigma}_{h}\in V_{h} such that

(6.4) a⁡(vhσ,φh)=0∀φh∈Vh,\displaystyle a(v^{\sigma}_{h},\varphi_{h})=0\qquad\forall\varphi_{h}\in V_{h},

and we have the near-best approximation bound

‖vσ−vhσ‖H1​(Y)≤ClCm​infwh∈Vh‖vσ−wh‖H1​(Y).\displaystyle\|v^{\sigma}-v^{\sigma}_{h}\|_{H^{1}(Y)}\leq\frac{C_{l}}{C_{m}}\inf_{w_{h}\in V_{h}}\|v^{\sigma}-w_{h}\|_{H^{1}(Y)}.

Choosing for VhV_{h} a Lagrange finite element space over a shape-regular triangulation 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} of Y¯\overline{Y} with mesh-size h>0h>0, consistent with the periodicity requirement, leads to a convergent method under mesh refinement. The discrete nonlinear system can be solved numerically using Howard’s algorithm (see e.g., [28]).

Introducing the approximate effective Hamiltonian

(6.5) H¯σ,h​(p):=∫Y(−σ​vhσ),\displaystyle\overline{H}_{\sigma,h}(p):=\int_{Y}(-\sigma v^{\sigma}_{h}),

we then have that

|H¯​(p)−H¯σ,h​(p)|≤|H¯​(p)−∫Y(−σ​vσ)|+σ​‖vσ−vhσ‖L1​(Y),\displaystyle\lvert\overline{H}(p)-\overline{H}_{\sigma,h}(p)\rvert\leq\left\lvert\overline{H}(p)-\int_{Y}(-\sigma v^{\sigma})\right\rvert+\sigma\|v^{\sigma}-v^{\sigma}_{h}\|_{L^{1}(Y)},

where ‖vσ−vhσ‖L1​(Y)→0\|v^{\sigma}-v^{\sigma}_{h}\|_{L^{1}(Y)}\rightarrow 0 as h→0h\rightarrow 0 and the first term on the right-hand side is of order O⁡(σ)O(\sigma) by Lemma 6.1.

6.2.3. Fourth-order-type variational formulation for (6.2)

If information on second-order derivatives of vσv^{\sigma} is desired, it is interesting to see that inspired by arguments based on Cordes-type conditions (see e.g., [4, 13, 28, 29]), we can derive a fourth-order-type variational formulation for vσv^{\sigma}, allowing for the construction of H2H^{2}-conforming finite element schemes. Introducing γ:=4​σ|b|2+4​σ∈C⁡(𝕋n×Λ,(0,1])\gamma:=\frac{4\sigma}{\lvert b\rvert^{2}+4\sigma}\in C(\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\Lambda,(0,1]), note that vσv^{\sigma} is the Y-periodic solution to

G⁡[vσ]=0,whereG⁡[w]:=supα∈Λ{γ⁡(⋅,α)​(−Δ​w−b⁡(⋅,α)⋅D​w+σ​w−g⁡(⋅,α))},\displaystyle G[v^{\sigma}]=0,\quad\text{where}\quad G[w]:=\sup_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\left\{\gamma(\cdot,\alpha)\left(-\Delta w-b(\cdot,\alpha)\cdot Dw+\sigma w-g(\cdot,\alpha)\right)\right\},

and vσv^{\sigma} is the unique element in Hper2​(Y)H^{2}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y) satisfying

a~​(vσ,φ):=(G⁡[vσ],σ​φ−Δ​φ)L2​(Y)=0∀φ∈Hper2​(Y).\displaystyle\tilde{a}(v^{\sigma},\varphi):=(G[v^{\sigma}],\sigma\varphi-\Delta\varphi)_{L^{2}(Y)}=0\qquad\forall\varphi\in H^{2}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y).

Indeed, note that due to (6.3) we have that a~\tilde{a} is strongly monotone: For any u1,u2∈Hper2​(Y)u_{1},u_{2}\in H^{2}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y), writing δu:=u1−u2\delta_{u}:=u_{1}-u_{2} and η:=4​σ−‖b‖∞24​σ+‖b‖∞2∈(0,1]\eta:=\frac{4\sigma-\|b\|_{\infty}^{2}}{4\sigma+\|b\|_{\infty}^{2}}\in(0,1], we have

|G[u1]\displaystyle\lvert G[u_{1}] −G[u2]−(σδu−Δδu)|2\displaystyle-G[u_{2}]-(\sigma\delta_{u}-\Delta\delta_{u})\rvert^{2}
≤supα∈Λ|−(γ⁡(⋅,α)−1)​Δ​δu−[γ​b]​(⋅,α)⋅D​δu+(γ⁡(⋅,α)−1)​σ​δu|2\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\ \lvert-(\gamma(\cdot,\alpha)-1)\Delta\delta_{u}-[\gamma b](\cdot,\alpha)\cdot D\delta_{u}+(\gamma(\cdot,\alpha)-1)\sigma\delta_{u}\rvert^{2}
≤(1−η)​(|Δ​δu|2+2​σ​|D​δu|2+σ2​|δu|2)\displaystyle\leq(1-\eta)(\lvert\Delta\delta_{u}\rvert^{2}+2\sigma\lvert D\delta_{u}\rvert^{2}+\sigma^{2}\lvert\delta_{u}\rvert^{2})

almost everywhere (note 2​|γ−1|2+12​σ​|γ​b|2=2−2​γ≤1−η2\lvert\gamma-1\rvert^{2}+\frac{1}{2\sigma}\lvert\gamma b\rvert^{2}=2-2\gamma\leq 1-\eta), and

‖Δ​δu‖L2​(Y)2+2​σ​‖D​δu‖L2​(Y)2+σ2​‖δu‖L2​(Y)2=‖σ​δu−Δ​δu‖L2​(Y)2,\displaystyle\|\Delta\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}+2\sigma\|D\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}+\sigma^{2}\|\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}=\|\sigma\delta_{u}-\Delta\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2},

which in combination yields

a~​(u1,δu)−a~​(u2,δu)≥(1−1−η)​‖σ​δu−Δ​δu‖L2​(Y)2.\displaystyle\tilde{a}(u_{1},\delta_{u})-\tilde{a}(u_{2},\delta_{u})\geq\left(1-\sqrt{1-\eta}\right)\|\sigma\delta_{u}-\Delta\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}^{2}.

Further, a~\tilde{a} satisfies the Lipschitz property

|a~​(u1,φ)−a~​(u2,φ)|≤(1−η+2)​‖σ​δu−Δ​δu‖L2​(Y)​‖σ​φ−Δ​φ‖L2​(Y).\displaystyle\lvert\tilde{a}(u_{1},\varphi)-\tilde{a}(u_{2},\varphi)\rvert\leq\left(\sqrt{1-\eta}+\sqrt{2}\right)\|\sigma\delta_{u}-\Delta\delta_{u}\|_{L^{2}(Y)}\|\sigma\varphi-\Delta\varphi\|_{L^{2}(Y)}.

Let Vh⊂Hper2​(Y)V_{h}\subset H^{2}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y) be a closed linear subspace of Hper2​(Y)H^{2}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y). By the Browder-Minty theorem and standard conforming Galerkin arguments, there exists a unique vhσ∈Vhv^{\sigma}_{h}\in V_{h} such that

a~​(vhσ,φh)=0∀φh∈Vh,\displaystyle\tilde{a}(v^{\sigma}_{h},\varphi_{h})=0\qquad\forall\varphi_{h}\in V_{h},

and, introducing the norm ‖|w|‖:=‖σ​w−Δ​w‖L2​(Y)|||w|||:=\|\sigma w-\Delta w\|_{L^{2}(Y)} for w∈Hper2​(Y)w\in H^{2}_{\mathrm{per}}(Y), we have the near-best approximation bound

‖|vσ−vhσ|‖≤1−η+21−1−η​infwh∈Vh‖|vσ−wh|‖.\displaystyle|||v^{\sigma}-v^{\sigma}_{h}|||\leq\frac{\sqrt{1-\eta}+\sqrt{2}}{1-\sqrt{1-\eta}}\inf_{w_{h}\in V_{h}}|||v^{\sigma}-w_{h}|||.

Choosing for VhV_{h} an Argyris or HCT finite element space over a shape-regular triangulation 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} of Y¯\overline{Y} with mesh-size h>0h>0, consistent with the periodicity requirement, leads to a convergent method under mesh refinement. The discrete nonlinear system can again be solved numerically using Howard’s algorithm. With the observations of this subsection at hand, one can also construct mixed finite element schemes and discontinuous Galerkin finite element schemes for (6.2) similarly to [13, 17].

6.2.4. Numerical experiments

For our numerical tests, we consider one linear example with known effective Hamiltonian and one nonlinear example with unknown effective Hamiltonian. For both tests, we use the method from Section 6.2.2.

Example 12.

Consider H:𝕋2×ℝ2→ℝH:\mathbb{T}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} given by (6.1) with n=2n=2 and Λ:={0}\Lambda:=\{0\}. We set b⁡(y,α):=b~​(y):=(12​π​cos⁡(2​π​y1),0)b(y,\alpha):=\tilde{b}(y):=\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\cos(2\pi y_{1}),0\right) and f⁡(y,α):=f~​(y)=1+sin⁡(2​π​y1)f(y,\alpha):=\tilde{f}(y)=1+\sin(2\pi y_{1}) for y=(y1,y2)∈𝕋2y=(y_{1},y_{2})\in\mathbb{T}^{2} and α∈Λ\alpha\in\Lambda. Our goal is to approximate the value of the effective Hamiltonian H¯\overline{H} at the point p:=(3,1)p:=(3,1), and compute the approximation error |H¯​(p)−H¯σ,h​(p)|\lvert\overline{H}(p)-\overline{H}_{\sigma,h}(p)\rvert, where the true value can be explicitly computed as

H¯​(p)=1+∫01sin⁡(2​π​t)​exp⁡(14​π2​sin⁡(2​π​t))​𝑑t∫01exp⁡(14​π2​sin⁡(2​π​s))​𝑑s.\displaystyle\overline{H}(p)=1+\frac{\int_{0}^{1}\sin(2\pi t)\exp(\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\sin(2\pi t))\,\mathrm{d}t}{\int_{0}^{1}\exp(\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\sin(2\pi s))\,\mathrm{d}s}.

In our numerical experiment, we compute H¯σ,h​(p)\overline{H}_{\sigma,h}(p) via (6.4)–(6.5), where we choose VhV_{h} to consist of continuous YY-periodic piecewise affine functions on a periodic shape-regular triangulation 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} of Y¯\overline{Y} into triangles with vertices {(i​h,j​h)}1≤i,j≤N\{(ih,jh)\}_{1\leq i,j\leq N} where N=1h∈ℕN=\frac{1}{h}\in\mathbb{N}. We choose σ=10−i\sigma=10^{-i} for i∈[−3,2]∩ℤi\in[-3,2]\cap\mathbb{Z} and h=2−jh=2^{-j} for j∈[1,10]∩ℤj\in[1,10]\cap\mathbb{Z}. The results are shown in Figure 6.1. Numerically, we can observe that the rate O⁡(σ)O(\sigma) in Lemma 6.1 is optimal.

Example 13.

We consider H:𝕋2×ℝ2→ℝH:\mathbb{T}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} given by (6.1) with n=2n=2 and Λ:={α∈ℝ2:|α|≤1}\Lambda:=\{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:|\alpha|\leq 1\}. We set b​(y,α):=b~​(y)+αb(y,\alpha):=\tilde{b}(y)+\alpha and f​(y,α):=f~​(y)f(y,\alpha):=\tilde{f}(y) for (y,α)∈𝕋2×Λ(y,\alpha)\in\mathbb{T}^{2}\times\Lambda, where b~\tilde{b} and f~\tilde{f} are defined as in Example 12. Note that H⁡(y,p)=|p|−b~​(y)⋅p−f~​(y)H(y,p)=|p|-\tilde{b}(y)\cdot p-\tilde{f}(y) for (y,p)∈𝕋2×ℝ2(y,p)\in\mathbb{T}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}. Our goal is to approximate the unknown effective Hamiltonian H¯\overline{H} on [−1,1]2[-1,1]^{2}. To this end, we approximate H¯​(p)\overline{H}(p) at all points pp in S:={±1,±34,±12,±38,±14,±18,0}2S:=\{\pm 1,\pm\frac{3}{4},\pm\frac{1}{2},\pm\frac{3}{8},\pm\frac{1}{4},\pm\frac{1}{8},0\}^{2}, where we chose a finer resolution around the origin. In our numerical experiment, we compute H¯σ,h​(p)\overline{H}_{\sigma,h}(p) via (6.4)–(6.5), where we choose VhV_{h} to consist of continuous YY-periodic piecewise affine functions on a periodic shape-regular triangulation 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} of Y¯\overline{Y} into triangles with vertices {(i​h,j​h)}1≤i,j≤N\{(ih,jh)\}_{1\leq i,j\leq N} where N=1h∈ℕN=\frac{1}{h}\in\mathbb{N}. We fixed a fine mesh, i.e., h=2−10h=2^{-10}, and produced convergence histories with respect to σ\sigma at each point p∈Sp\in S. The nonlinear discrete problems were solved using Howard’s algorithm. For the plot of the numerical effective Hamiltonian we used σ=2−4\sigma=2^{-4}; see Figure 6.2 (A). An exemplary convergence history of |H¯σ,h​(p)−H¯σ2,h​(p)|\lvert\overline{H}_{\sigma,h}(p)-\overline{H}_{\frac{\sigma}{2},h}(p)\rvert with respect to σ\sigma, for p=(−1,−1)p=(-1,-1), is shown in Figure 6.2 (B) and we observe the rate O⁡(σ)O(\sigma), as expected.
